covenants::htlc: add try_parse_htlc + canonical observability types
Contributed by Ziyang (as exfer-stack) upstream to ahuman-exfer/exfer, the Exfer chain itself.
https://github.com/ahuman-exfer/exfer/pull/20

## Summary

Adds two pieces of public API to `exfer::covenants::htlc`:

1. **`try_parse_htlc(&[u8]) -> Option<HtlcParams>`** — the inverse of the existing public `htlc(...)` constructor.
2. **Canonical wire types** for HTLC lifecycle observation: `HtlcState`, `HtlcRole`, `HtlcParams`, `HtlcClaimRecord`, `HtlcReclaimRecord`, `HtlcRecord`.

Purely additive. No protocol change, no on-chain change, no behavioural change to `htlc(...)`, no new dependencies. No version / `RELEASE_TAG` bump — happy to follow whatever release scheme you decide for this on merge.

## Why

`covenants::htlc::htlc(...)` has been public since the initial release — it lets anyone build an HTLC output script. The natural inverse — given an output script, recover its four parameters — has been missing.

Anyone wanting to observe HTLCs on-chain (block explorers, light wallets, atomic-swap counterparties verifying the commitment they were promised, audit tooling) currently has to either:

- Re-implement the script parser by inspecting the AST shape themselves, or
- Maintain their own parallel `HtlcRecord`-shaped JSON and accept silent drift if `htlc(...)` ever changes its internal composition.

Both are footguns: if the upstream template ever changes a combinator arrangement, every downstream parser silently breaks. Providing the inverse alongside the constructor, in the same module, keeps everyone in lockstep with whatever bytes `htlc(...)` produces.

The wire types address a related issue. Anyone serialising HTLC lifecycle state has to invent their own JSON shape for `(state, role, claim/reclaim detail, lock_block_height, amount, ...)`. Without a canonical set, two projects observing the same chain produce subtly different JSON — different field names, different enum spellings, different hex casing — and clients have to special-case each. Defining the shapes once in this crate gives every observer a common vocabulary that is necessarily consistent with the constructor.

## Implementation

`try_parse_htlc` works as follows:

1. Deserialise the bytes to a `Program` AST via `script::serialize::deserialize_program`.
2. Walk every `Combinator::Const` node and collect the candidate constants. The template embeds exactly two 32-byte `Value::Bytes` (the pubkeys), one `Value::Hash` (the hashlock), and one `Value::U64` (the timeout). If the counts don't match, return `None`.
3. For each of the two possible `(sender, receiver)` orderings, reconstruct the program via `htlc(sender, receiver, hash_lock, timeout)` and compare its serialised bytes against the input. Return the first ordering whose bytes match.

The byte-for-byte equality check is what makes the function sound: a `Some(params)` return is a proof that the input is exactly `htlc(params.sender, params.receiver, Hash256(params.hash_lock), params.timeout_height)`. Structurally-similar-but-non-canonical scripts that happen to embed the right constants in different positions are rejected because the reconstruction won't match.
